title: The Glory Be
hook: the shortest Catholic prayer, praise to the three persons
carry: as it was in the beginning
tomorrow: The Apostles' Creed, line by line

segments.voice: Yesterday, knees and bows: to genuflect is to bend the knee. Your line was the body says it first. What did your posture say? And today is a milestone. Day one hundred.

Day one hundred. If you've come this far, you've kept at something for over three months, and that deserves a moment. So here's a fitting thing for it: a prayer that takes about seven seconds. It closes each decade of the rosary. It ends the psalms when monks and nuns and priests pray their daily hours. It fits in the gap between one task and the next. It asks for nothing. It doesn't confess anything. It just gives glory, and goes back to work. Today: the Glory Be.
screen: `ONE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `A SEVEN-SECOND PRAYER.` → `IT ASKS FOR NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in its traditional English form: "Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen." Many Catholics today say Holy Spirit. In the old Latin: Gloria Patri, et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto. Sicut erat in principio, et nunc, et semper, et in saecula saeculorum. Amen. Today's word is the name for a prayer like this: doxology. From two Greek words: doxa, glory, and logos, word. A glory-word. The Gloria at Mass is called the greater doxology, and this one the lesser. Look at its shape. The first line is the sign of the cross from three days ago, turned from a name into praise: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. The second line is all about time. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be. Past, present, future, in one breath. And some readers hear a history in that line. Christians once argued fiercely over whether the Son had always existed or had a beginning. Read that way, praying that the glory was the same in the beginning is a way of saying, every day: he always was. A seven-second prayer, carrying an old argument, settled into rhythm. The last phrase, world without end, is the old English way of saying forever: in the Latin, into the ages of ages. Catholics use the Glory Be the way you'd use a period at the end of a sentence. After a psalm. After a decade. After a task. It closes things, and hands them back.
screen: `DOXA AND LOGOS: A GLORY-WORD.` · `FATHER, SON AND HOLY SPIRIT.` · `PAST, PRESENT, FUTURE.` · `AN OLD ARGUMENT IN SEVEN SECONDS.` · then, large: `AS IT WAS IN THE BEGINNING, IS NOW, AND EVER SHALL BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: close something. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you finished today, or will finish soon. A report, a load of laundry, a hard conversation. When it's done, before you move to the next thing, stop for seven seconds. If you pray, say the Glory Be over it. If you don't, simply mark the end: done, and let it go. For now, just sit with the feeling of something finished. The bell holds the time.
Doxology. A glory-word: a short prayer of praise, like the Glory Be, to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: as it was in the beginning. Today, at the end of one task, pause for seven seconds before starting the next. Day one hundred.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Glory Be at the end of each decade of the rosary and after the psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, and many say it on its own at the end of a task or a day.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): quoted Glory Be now matches the cited Book of Common Prayer 1662 words ('Holy Ghost'), with a note that many Catholics say 'Holy Spirit'; 'two days ago' corrected to three (the sign of the cross was day 97); 'the Mass has a big one' made precise (the Gloria, the greater doxology); the Arian link and its 'three hundreds' date softened to 'some readers hear'; 'kids learn it right after...' and 'so often they barely hear it' cut.

The traditional English Glory Be is quoted in full in the voice (with 'Holy Spirit'; older Catholic books say 'Holy Ghost'). It is an old traditional text; the cited public-domain English form is the Book of Common Prayer 1662 wording of the same prayer. Confirm the Keeper is happy with this form.
Latin text of the Gloria Patri given from memory; confirm.
The link between 'sicut erat in principio' and the Arian controversy is commonly stated but debated; phrased as 'that line has a history'. Confirm.
'Lesser doxology' (Glory Be) vs 'greater doxology' (the Gloria at Mass): stated as 'often called the little one'. Confirm.
